faq.answer: No. You can examine a principle's reasons and application and deliberately retain it. Greater willingness does not guarantee that every belief has been reviewed, and review does not require repeated changes of position.
faq.question: Does stronger Values mean having no principles?

faq.answer: The conclusion alone does not establish it. A traditional position may have been reconsidered and retained. Look at what happens when relevant reasons are available and there is a usable opportunity to consider them.
faq.question: Does a traditional position show weaker Values?

faq.answer: Yes. Understanding a reason does not require accepting its conclusion. You can identify a factual problem, a different priority, or a personal boundary. A facet label should not be used to pressure anyone into agreement.
faq.question: Can I understand an opposing view and still disagree?

faq.answer: That would be too broad a claim. Related IPIP Liberalism scales contain political and religious items, so their measurement content needs to be distinguished. This guide still cannot determine an individual's political identity, religion, voting choice, or moral standing.
faq.question: Is Values entirely unrelated to political positions?

faq.answer: It may clarify the reasons you are considering, but it may also be only a response to an exercise. Keep arranged practice separate from natural review, check the argument fairly, and decide whether to retain, revise, or suspend judgment. One exercise does not demonstrate a personality change.
faq.question: Will writing arguments against my view change this trait?

not_for: Do not use this page for clinical diagnosis or as the sole basis for hiring or admission.
method_boundary.summary: Use this page to understand personality concepts and examine everyday behavior. Interpret actual scores using the instrument’s scoring method, reference sample, and intended use.

sections.body:
In the NEO/IPIP-NEO vocabulary used on this site, Values concerns willingness to reexamine established beliefs, traditions, and social norms. It belongs to Openness to Experience. A familiar rule may prompt questions about its reasons, the needs it serves, and whether its application still fits the circumstances.

Review does not require abandonment. You can consider competing reasons and retain a commitment, change one condition, or postpone judgment while seeking information. Counting changes of opinion is therefore an inadequate shortcut. A stable conclusion does not, by itself, reveal an unwillingness to examine it.

Stronger, weaker, and middle descriptions refer to continuous differences rather than political or moral types. Stronger willingness does not mean that every belief has been carefully reviewed. Weaker willingness does not mean that reflection never occurs. The issue, the available opportunity, and the actual process all matter.
sections.heading: What happens when a familiar belief comes under review?

sections.body:
Your position is what you currently support. Examination concerns how you consider reasons for it and reasons against it. Two people can reach the same position through careful review, inherited assumptions, social pressure, or quite different experiences. The conclusion alone cannot identify the facet.

Moral judgment requires attention to actions, responsibilities, consequences, and ethical reasons. This facet is not a ranking of virtue. Reconsidering a norm does not establish that someone treats people well, and respecting a tradition does not establish prejudice. Examination also does not require treating a harmful proposal as equally acceptable.

Agreement is a separate observation. You may say yes to preserve a relationship, avoid a penalty, or end an exhausting conversation. Those circumstances do not show voluntary reconsideration. You can also understand another person's reasoning, respect their boundaries, and still disagree.

Ideas concerns interest in concepts; Actions concerns unfamiliar activities. A taste for debate or a varied lifestyle cannot establish that you have examined your own commitments.
sections.heading: A position, a moral judgment, and agreement answer different questions

sections.body:
Some disagreements turn on a factual assumption that can be checked. Others turn on the relative weight of continuity, fairness, freedom, care, or another valued concern. People can agree on the facts and still choose differently because they prioritize those concerns differently.

For one belief, ask what you think is happening, what principle you want to protect, and whether the current rule is the only way to protect it. That makes the possible exits clearer: correct a factual assumption, revise how a principle is applied, retain a reasoned priority, or acknowledge an unresolved conflict.

With stronger willingness, you may reopen such questions more readily. Whether the review is useful still depends on the quality of the reasons and the decision that is needed. With weaker willingness, you may initially rely on an established framework. Check what happens when an exception or changed condition actually arises rather than assuming either rigidity or reliable decisiveness.

Mixed patterns are possible. You might review institutional rules readily and rarely revisit a personal commitment. You might also examine a belief privately while declining to discuss it in a setting where disagreement carries a cost.
sections.heading: Separate factual assumptions from competing priorities

sections.body:
Imagine a volunteer group whose rule says that every meeting must be attended in person. One member values equal participation and initially supports the rule. When a member with limited transport explains the difficulty, the first member considers whether physical presence is the best available measure of participation. They support a remote option while keeping the expectation that everyone contributes.

The informative part is the consideration of the original reason and the changed circumstances. Supporting the new option could also result from friendship, pressure from the coordinator, or a wish to end the dispute. The decision alone does not separate these explanations.

A natural counterexample might be another routine group rule, discussed without pressure and with relevant information, where the same person declines to consider any alternative. That would narrow a broad description of willingness to review norms. It would not erase the earlier episode.

Conversely, a person known for retaining group traditions may voluntarily examine a proposal and still reject it because an important practical concern remains unanswered. Keeping the rule is compatible with having reviewed it. These are illustrative situations, not a measurement of a real participant.
sections.heading: A revised rule can preserve the original principle

sections.body:
Look back at low-stakes disagreements that occurred naturally. Note the original judgment, the different reason you encountered, whether you chose to investigate it, what facts you checked, what priorities remained in conflict, and what you retained or changed. A public statement and private review need not match.

Distinguish an available, reasonably safe opportunity followed by examination; an available opportunity where examination did not occur; and no usable opportunity. Missing information, immediate time pressure, or the realistic cost of expressing disagreement may prevent an informative observation. Forced agreement should be recorded as pressure rather than evidence of openness.

Provisionally retain a limited hypothesis if several comparable natural episodes show voluntary consideration of unfamiliar reasons. Narrow it if that happens only with particular topics or when little is personally at stake. Set the facet interpretation aside when appeasement, pressure, or a major information gap explains the record more directly.

Not finding a counterexample means that none was found in the situations considered. It does not establish that you always behave this way. A brief record can refine an account of your experiences, but cannot validate a personality trait or another person's moral character.
sections.heading: Observe the process, including opportunities that were absent

sections.body:
Choose a routine norm you can examine without putting an important relationship or obligation at risk. Write down its purpose, the factual assumptions supporting its current form, a relevant exception, and the costs of an alternative. Represent the alternative accurately; you do not need to invent respectable reasons for unsupported claims.

Choose an explicit next step. Retain the current practice and explain why, revise its application, or defer the conclusion until a named piece of information is available. If an agreement is needed now, state what will happen meanwhile and what would justify reopening it.

Record this as an arranged exercise, separately from naturally occurring review. Evaluate whether you understood the reasons, separated facts from priorities, and reached an explainable next step. Completing the exercise does not show that the facet increased, and keeping your original position is not a failed attempt.
sections.heading: Conduct one review without making agreement the goal

sections.body:
The [official IPIP comparison](https://ipip.ori.org/newNEO_FacetsTable.htm) pairs NEO Values with IPIP Liberalism as similar constructs. The [long-form items](https://ipip.ori.org/newNEOFacetsKey.htm) and [Maples short form](https://ipip.ori.org/30FacetNEO-PI-RItems_Maples_etal.htm) contain political and religious positions. They cannot accurately be described as measuring only a position-free examination process.

This page uses Values to explain willingness to revisit beliefs. It is not a description of every related instrument's items, nor a basis for assigning a reader a political identity, religion, or voting choice. A particular result needs the relevant instrument, version, and interpretation rules; a public explanation cannot supply an unreported measurement.

The [BFI-2 authors' page](https://www.ocf.berkeley.edu/~johnlab/bfi.html) also uses Open-Mindedness as a broader domain name. That domain, everyday open-mindedness, and the Values facet should not be exchanged simply because their names sound similar. These sources establish terminology and instrument distinctions, not FermatMind product validation.
sections.heading: Related labels do not imply identical measurements

sections.body:
For the broader domain, read [Openness to Experience](/en/personality/big-five/openness). For interest in conceptual discussion, read [Ideas](/en/personality/big-five/facets/ideas). For unfamiliar activities, read [Actions](/en/personality/big-five/facets/actions).

[Imagination](/en/personality/big-five/facets/imagination), [Aesthetics](/en/personality/big-five/facets/aesthetics), and [Feelings](/en/personality/big-five/facets/feelings) address other areas of experience. The [30-facet guide](/en/personality/big-five/facets) explains the vocabulary without turning one observed pattern into results for the other facets.
sections.heading: Continue with the part of openness you mean
